opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think of it less as a tool and more as a very fast, very well-read junior collaborator who never gets tired. In my day-to-day work, a lot of time goes into things that aren't the core research question: writing experiment scaffolding, debugging data pipelines, reading through a pile of papers to see whether someone has already tried an idea. That's where it's most useful. I can describe what I want, it drafts the code or summarizes the related work, and I spend my energy checking and deciding rather than typing.

But I try to be careful about where the boundary is. For the parts that really matter, like choosing which direction to bet on, judging whether a result is real or just noise, or deciding how to design a training recipe, I don't think you can hand that over. Models are very good at producing something that looks plausible, and in research, plausible-but-wrong is the most dangerous kind of output. So my habit is to treat what it gives me as a strong first draft, and then verify everything that will actually drive a decision.

What's interesting is that it's changed how I think about my own role. If execution gets cheaper, then taste becomes more important: knowing which questions are worth asking, and noticing when something is off. In a way, working with these systems pushes you to be more of a researcher and less of an engineer, which I think is a good thing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's changed how I spend my day. I used to think of these models as an autocomplete with better manners. Now I think of OpenClaude more like a very fast junior colleague who has read everything but hasn't yet built the taste to know which of the ten plausible approaches is the right one.

Where it's most useful is in the parts of research that are tedious but necessary. Writing the data pipeline. Reproducing a baseline from a paper where the authors' code doesn't quite run. Sketching five variants of an ablation so I can look at them side by side before committing. Those used to eat whole afternoons, and now they take an hour, and I get to spend the afternoon actually thinking about the experiment.

Where I've learned to be careful is anywhere judgment matters more than execution. It will give you a confident answer about why a training run diverged, and it may be right, but it may also just be pattern-matching to the most common explanation. So I treat it as a hypothesis generator, not a verdict. The discipline is: it proposes, I verify. If I skip the verification step because the answer sounds smart, that's on me.

The thing that surprised me most is how it changes collaboration between people. When everyone on the team can prototype quickly, the bottleneck moves from "who can build this" to "who has the clearest idea of what's worth building." That's a healthier place for a research group to be, I think. It rewards clarity of thought over sheer stamina.

So my short answer is: enormously useful, as long as you remember it's a collaborator and not an oracle. The moment you stop arguing with it, you've stopped doing research.
